chapter: Louis Jordan, Ink Spots and the union
title: Lathing with his father between music jobs
summary: He did house lathing with his dad and brother when music work got lean, using a hatchet and nailing fast.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Have you belonged to any other unions, besides the musicians? Like you said the other day you used to do like lathe?
Lathing?
Lathing.
No, I didn't belong to no union.
You didn't belong to the union.
No.
Roofers' or contractors' or carpenters' or anything like that.
No. See, because I was working with my
dad.
Oh, I see.
He would get the jobs and have me go on them, and me and my brother would go on them and finish them up, you know, during the week, and we'd go ahead and do three houses a week.
Uh-huh.
You know.
So you used to do -- is that what your dad used to do, like small contracting --
Yeah.
-- jobs and stuff.
Uh-huh.
That's really a good profession, really, because there's always some work around, you know.
Oh, yeah. They're building.
Yeah. Because if people aren't building something new they can be remodeling or --
That's right.
-- building extensions, or --
Yeah, he kept busy.
So you did that, like in the '30s, when things would get lean, you know.
Yeah.
When you weren't getting that much work.
What?
You did that sort of like to fall back on when you weren't --
I done it any time I got the chance to do it, to tell you the truth.
Yeah. To get the money together.
To get the money together, yeah. Lathing.
Lathing all the way to the bank.
That's right. We'd get on a house, oh, boy, as big as this house here, I'd say.
Uh-huh.

My goodness, we'd start early in the morning, about 7:00 o'clock. This house would be finished by the time 4:00 o'clock would come, we'd be through working. The house would be finished. Ready to start another one.
You had to watch out for your fingers, though, right?
Huh?
You've got to watch out for your fingers.
To tell you the truth, I never did hit my fingers.
Oh, yeah?
Yeah. I had a hatchet.
Boy, I'll tell you, I had to watch --
when I played basketball I had to watch it. It's no game for a guitarist.
I had a hatchet.
One of those things with a hammer on one side and a hatchet on the other, one of those?
No hammer at all, just a hatchet.
How come?
Because the hammer was on the end of the hatchet.
That's what I mean, yeah.
Yeah. So all you had to do was turn the hatchet, you know, and nail it. I'd do ceilings like I was doing this (Unintelligible). People'd think I was eating dye by the time I got through work.
From the nails.
From the nails, yes. You never done that kind.
